intro: Mahler follows the funeral march with an A-minor storm, torn open by a cello lament. Near the end, the brass find a magnificent D-major chorale — and lose it again.

sections.label: A · Running basses and slashing chords
sections.mNote: Low strings hurl a five-note figure against orchestral blows

sections.label: B · Cellos recall the funeral march
sections.mNote: F minor, at the first movement’s slower tempo

sections.label: A′ · The running strings return
sections.mNote: The opening figures break back into the cello lament

sections.label: B′ · Cellos over a timpani roll
sections.mNote: A long E♭-minor song with scarcely any accompaniment

sections.label: Dev · March and storm collide
sections.mNote: Trumpet figures and the funeral tune cross in the orchestra

sections.label: C · Brass chorale in D major
sections.mNote: Long brass chords above racing strings and harp

sections.label: Coda · The storm returns in scraps
sections.mNote: Short string figures survive the fading brass chorale

cues.title: Five notes strike upwards
cues.text: Low strings fling up a five-note figure. The orchestra answers with slashing diminished-seventh chords, and the strings try again. Mahler asks for the greatest possible vehemence. This is the funeral march’s anger let loose.
cues.evidence: Peters full score, plate 9015, p. 48; Lew Smoley identifies the opening bass figure and diminished-seventh chords: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-2-sturmisch-bewegt-mit-groster-vehemenz/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos remember the march
cues.text: The rapid woodwind notes run out, leaving a timpani roll. In F minor, the cellos begin a lament. Mahler explicitly restores the tempo of the first movement’s funeral march; its tune has followed us into the storm.
cues.evidence: Peters score, pp. 57–58, rehearsal 5: Bedeutend langsamer, im Tempo des ersten Satzes Trauermarsch. Smoley identifies F minor and the cello theme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two summers at Maiernigg
cues.text: Mahler begins the Fifth in the summer of 1901. By the time he returns to Maiernigg the next summer, he has met and married Alma Schindler, and they are expecting their first child. The symphony takes shape across those two summers.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction: composition in 1901–02 and the family chronology. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: Twenty bars for cellos
cues.text: The cellos stretch a small sigh into a long E♭-minor song. For twenty bars, almost nothing accompanies them: a timpani roll, then a held G♭ in the violas. The orchestra has left them an enormous empty room.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the second slow passage in E♭ minor, the twenty-bar cello line, the continuing timpani roll and the viola G♭.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The brass find D major
cues.text: Trumpets and trombones open out into D major. The brass sing a chorale in long notes while strings and harp keep sweeping beneath them. Mahler crowns it with a chord marked as the high point of the movement.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 102 and following pages; Smoley describes the D-major chorale, string and harp accompaniment, and the chord marked Höhepunkt.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The storm has survived
cues.text: As the chorale fades, scraps of the opening creep into strings and brass. The woodwinds release another shower of descending triplets. The D-major hymn will have to wait until the finale to close the symphony.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 107 onwards. Smoley describes the return of the opening motifs after the chorale and the chorale’s later recovery in the finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harp notes in the wreckage
cues.text: The last pages scatter little wind and harp notes among pale string figures. The opening’s furious phrases have dwindled to scraps. Three low notes descend towards the close; the last belongs to the timpani.
cues.evidence: Peters score, closing pages, including p. 116; Smoley identifies the sparse wind and harp notes and the final descending bass notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A timpani roll, then the cellos
transitions.from: A · Running basses and slashing chords
transitions.to: B · Cellos recall the funeral march
transitions.how: The woodwinds’ racing notes dwindle to a stop over a quiet timpani roll. Mahler slows to the first movement’s funeral-march tempo and turns to F minor. Cellos sing the march-derived melody, with short wind figures still flickering around it.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, pp. 57–58; Smoley’s guide identifies the thinning woodwinds, timpani roll, key and cello melody.

transitions.title: The woodwinds bring back the storm
transitions.from: B · Cellos recall the funeral march
transitions.how: A rising cello phrase reaches a strained dominant-seventh chord in the brass. Rapid chromatic woodwind figures break in, and the violins recover the fanfare-like theme. Timpani hammer its rising and falling thirds beneath them.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the end of the first slow span and the abbreviated return of the opening music.

transitions.title: The timpani roll stays behind
transitions.to: B′ · Cellos over a timpani roll
transitions.how: The woodwinds race to a halt again. A timpani roll continues beneath the cellos’ slower E♭-minor line; later the violas add a held G♭. A leap and falling second from the storm become the beginning of a long song.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide, second slow section: E♭ minor, twenty-bar cello arioso, timpani roll and viola G♭.

transitions.title: D major opens above the strings
transitions.to: C · Brass chorale in D major
transitions.how: Rising figures drive towards a broad D-major statement in trumpets and trombones. The strings turn their rushing notes into scales and arpeggios, reinforced by harp, while the brass extend the melody into a chorale.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 102; Smoley describes the D-major arrival and its brass, string and harp writing.

transitions.title: Short figures invade the chorale
transitions.from: C · Brass chorale in D major
transitions.to: Coda · The storm returns in scraps
transitions.how: The D-major brass chords subside. The opening five-note figure returns in fragments among strings and brass, then woodwind triplets restore the falling chromatic lines. Another short outburst follows before the harp and scattered strings are left to finish.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 107 to the end; Smoley describes the fading chorale, returning opening motifs and sparse coda.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, II, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed p. 48: rushing low strings and orchestral attacks; pp. 57–58: slow cello melody; p. 102: brass chorale; pp. 107–116: withdrawal and coda.

timeline.note: Running low strings and bassoons meet sharp orchestral attacks.
The woodwind figures soften above held notes in the lower instruments.
Cellos sing the slower melody, with sparse woodwinds and bass punctuation.
The brass chorale opens above moving strings and harp.
Brass chords and low instruments fade after the chorale.
Quiet upper strings, scraps of woodwind melody and isolated harp notes finish the movement.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
